name: Papyrus sheet
kb: Cut, layered and pressed papyrus strips
note: Papyrus does not cure; it works wet. Plant laminae naturally adhere without paste if pressed fresh.

name: Parchment sheet
note: Scraped skin accepts ink and erasure. Alkali lime wash removes hair without destroying fibre.

name: Rag paper sheet
kb: Rag pulp made into sheets by felting
note: China's invention: pulp beaten finer until felts into sheet on screen, without pressing to hardness.

name: Quill pen
note: The split must hold capillary action. Quills need re-splitting every few hours.

name: Steel pen nib
note: Stamping gives consistency; hardening to spring temper is critical. Mass production beats quill sharpening.

name: Fountain pen
kb: Sealed ink reservoir with capillary feed and nib
note: Ink reservoir under the nib, with capillary feed. Early designs leak; improved feeds (Waterman, Parker) in the 1880s fix this. Replaces dip pens and quills. Refillable or cartridge designs follow; mass production drives prices down.

name: Graphite pencil
note: Graphite hardens in proportion to clay; German recipe ratios and kiln control took centuries to perfect.

name: Carbon paper
note: Coating must be even without clogging pores. Wax carrier keeps carbon from smudging.

name: Iron gall ink
note: Tannin in galls binds iron to cellulose chemically. This is why medieval manuscripts survive.

name: Printing ink, oil-based
kb: Linseed oil with carbon black, boiled with resin
note: Carbon in heated linseed oil. Sticks to metal type. Water-based ink beads off metal, non-obvious blocker.

name: Woodblock printing
note: Chinese invention: carving mirror image freehand requires skill. Hardest part is cutting fine lines that do not splinter.

name: Movable type, cast metal
note: Gutenberg's invention was the punch, matrix and adjustable mould that cast thousands of identical letters to same body height.

name: Punch and matrix for type
note: Single punch makes many matrices; each must be struck vertically and squared. Precision is the barrier.

name: Adjustable type mould
note: Width must adjust to cast all letters to same body height. Ejection must not deform cooling metal.

name: Type metal alloy
kb: Lead-tin-antimony alloy with low melting point and high hardness
note: Lead alone is too soft; tin raises hardness. Antimony prevents shrinking as it cools.

name: Composing stick
note: Compositors set metal sorts in stick, proof, transfer to galley. Allows rearrangement before lock-up.

name: Chase and forme
note: Type must lock so tightly quoins cannot shift under press pressure. Wood swells; metal wedges must be wedged.

name: Screw press for printing
note: Screw threads must be clean or they strip. Parallel guides prevent binding. Arm length trades speed for force.

name: Iron hand press
note: Cast iron strong in compression. Toggle linkage multiplies force near end of platen travel.

name: Cylinder press
kb: Paper fed between rotating cylinder and flat type bed, steam-driven
note: Rotating cylinder instead of platen. Type moves under rolling pressure. Faster, smoother. Steam power essential.

name: Rotary press
kb: Type or stereotypes on rotating cylinder, paper fed between cylinders, steam-driven
note: Two cylinders, type wraps around curved plate. Continuous feed and output. Thousands of sheets per hour.

name: Stereotype plate
kb: Papier-mache mould of type forme, cast into metal plate, allows curved mounting
note: Papier-mache matrix captures exact impression; pour must be fast. Curved plates enable rotary presses.

name: Electrotype plate
kb: Electroplated copper shell backed with lead, captures type forme detail
note: Copper deposits slowly and must be backed by lead to prevent buckling. Thinner than stereotype.

name: Linotype machine
kb: Keyboard-driven machine that casts entire lines of type as single metal slugs
note: Operator taps keyboard, matrices drop, spacing added, hot metal poured into mould. Complete line emerges cast solid.

name: Lithography
kb: Greasy image drawn on limestone, dampened and rolled with oily ink; ink sticks only to image
note: Greasy ink on stone, water-acidified alum applied. Water repels grease, grease rejects water. Non-obvious chemistry.

name: Chromolithography
note: Registration between plates must be accurate to fraction of millimetre. Hand-drawn art for each colour.

name: Offset lithography
kb: Lithographic image offset onto rubber blanket, then onto paper, allowing curved or small presses
note: Rubber blanket expensive but does not damage stone. Pressure halves; image reverses twice.

name: Halftone screen and dot matrix
note: THE invention making photographs printable. Cross-ruled screen photographed with image. Variable dots create tone illusion.

name: Photoengraving (relief)
note: Photo-resist captures halftone dots; acid etches between them. Height must be uniform.

name: Typewriter
kb: Keyboard-driven machine that stamps type bars onto paper through ribbon
note: Keyed strike-through ribbon. QWERTY deliberately slows typist to prevent jams. Shift key accesses capitals.

name: Shift key mechanism
note: Basket must move reliably without sticking. Spring return precise or next keystroke misses.

name: Stencil duplicator
note: Screen must hold fabric taut. Register sprockets prevent misalignment. 200 copies max before wear.

name: Mimeograph
note: Rotating drum distributes ink evenly. Stencil wears faster but runs extend from 200 to 2000.

name: Case binding
note: Sewing essential for durability; gluing alone fails in years. Raised bands protect sewing from shearing.

name: Camera obscura with lens
kb: Darkened box or room with lens projecting inverted image onto screen or ground glass
note: Lens must be good or image is dim. Pinhole too dim for anything but bright sunlight.

name: Camera lucida
note: Prism angle must be exactly 45 degrees. Artist traces outline, adds shading freehand.

name: Silver halide photographic sensitivity
note: Light breaks silver halide to silver metal; unexposed must be removed without darkening image.

name: Daguerreotype plate
kb: Polished copper plate coated with silver, sensitised with iodine vapour, exposed and developed with mercury
note: Polished copper plate, silver-coated, exposed to light, developed in mercury vapour. Mirror-like image. Cannot be copied.

name: Calotype paper negative
note: Negative allows unlimited prints. Paper texture shows in final. Toning with gold chloride prevents fading.

name: Wet collodion plate
kb: Nitrocellulose emulsion on glass, sensitised with silver nitrate, must be exposed and developed wet
note: Glass substrate better than paper. Emulsion must stay wet or sensitivity drops. Field photographers carried dark tents.

name: Dry gelatin emulsion plate
note: Silver halide in gelatin. Sensitive when dry. Long shelf life. Easy storage and transport. Portable photography practical.

name: Celluloid roll film
note: Transparent backing allows frame spacing with sprocket holes. Rolls hold 20-120 frames. Enables amateur photography.

name: Panchromatic emulsion
note: Orthochromatic sees only blue and green. Panchromatic needs red safelight, not yellow.

name: Autochrome colour plate
note: Viewing requires backlighting. Resolution is 100 lines per mm. Colours pastel. Only process before Kodachrome.

name: Flash powder
note: Magnesium produces blue-white light nearer daylight than gas. Burns in fraction of second.

name: Flashbulb
note: Oxygen must be pure and bulb sealed; any leak ruins it. One-use. Shutter speed rises to 1/500.

name: Leaf shutter
note: Blades must open fully then close evenly. Timing via gears. Flash fires when open.

name: Focal plane shutter
note: Slit width controls exposure. Fast speeds need very narrow slit. Above 1/500 require multiple slits.

name: Cine camera
note: Intermittent sprocket movement must be reliable. Spring or motor drive. Motor gives steadier speed.

name: Intermittent film movement
kb: Rotating Maltese cross cam drives film advance pin intermittently, pausing for exposure
note: Cross slots must be precise or pin binds. Smooth during pull-down allows high speed.

name: Film projector
note: Shutter blanks lens during pull-down to prevent flicker. Gate holds film flat. Heat dissipation critical.

name: Phonautograph
note: Records sound into grooves but cannot play back. Stylus must be flexible but not break.

name: Tin foil phonograph
note: Indents rather than cuts; playback faint. Surface crinkles after 10-20 plays.

name: Wax cylinder record
note: Wax gives 100+ plays. Cylinders can be shaved and recoated. Playback by needle vibration.

name: Disc record
note: Groove meanders side-to-side encoding amplitude. Shellac pressing from master. Playable from multiple copies.

name: Acoustic horn recording
note: Horn gain is logarithmic. Frequency response lumpy; bass absent. Diaphragm compliance limits force.

name: Gramophone motor and governor
note: Speed variation ruins pitch fidelity. Centrifugal governor adjusts throttle. Flywheel smooths ripple.

name: Carbon microphone
note: Packing pressure critical; too loose and sensitivity drops. Short lifetime; packing settles.

name: Moving coil loudspeaker
note: Paper cone is resonant; large speakers smooth response. Impedance 4-16 ohms.

name: Magnetic tape recording
note: Steel wire or tape magnetised by recording head. Erasable and reusable. Linear response superior to disc.

name: AC bias for tape recording
note: Without bias, distortion is severe. Bias frequency above 20 kHz. Bias level is critical.

name: Disc cutting lathe
note: Spiral feed pitch must be precise. Speed must be constant or pitch wavers. Stylus wear compensated.

name: Electric telegraph
kb: Key switch closes electromagnet circuit, solenoid pulls armature clicking against stop
note: Single needle precedes this. Relay allows weak signal to switch strong at repeater.

name: Morse key and sounder
note: Morse code uses short and long pulses. Sounder design affects learning; American style fast and bright.

name: Telegraph relay
note: Allows unlimited range. Weak local battery switches strong line battery. Contacts burn if dirty.

name: Submarine cable with gutta percha
note: The insulation IS the invention. Rubber perishes and cotton is useless wet, but gutta percha, the latex of Palaquium from Malaya, is thermoplastic: it softens in hot water, can be moulded round a copper core, sets hard, and does not rot in seawater. It is reached by extending east whatever long-distance ocean trade route you already have (Rome already sails to India annually; adapt to your own reach), so it is a trading problem, not an impossibility. The second, harder lesson is electrical: a long submerged cable is a capacitor, pulses smear into each other, and pushing more voltage at it destroys the insulation, which is what killed the first Atlantic cable in 1858. Signal slowly and detect sensitively.

name: Cable repeater and amplifier
note: Extends range from 100 to 1000+ km. Submerged repeaters hard to maintain.

name: Telephone transmitter
note: Louder than mouth against mouthpiece but prone to feedback. Requires constant voltage supply.

name: Telephone receiver
note: Fidelity poor; only 300-3400 Hz pass. Impedance must match handset. Diaphragm vibration violent but small amplitude.

name: Telephone exchange and switchboard
note: Operator hears both parties; must avoid feedback. Capacity limited to available operators.

name: Strowger automatic exchange
note: A caller dials pulses on the handset (1=one pulse, 2=two pulses, etc). These pulses drive a stepper motor which rotates a wiper across a grid of contacts, selecting the called party's line. No human operator needed. The 1890 Strowger exchange was a mechanical marvel: 100 stepper units could handle 10,000 lines. Reliability was marginal (mechanical wear, misalignment), but no wage bill. Replaced manual exchanges over 30 years. The real innovation is replacing human labor with electromechanics.

name: Loading coil
kb: Inductance coil added to telephone line at intervals, reduces attenuation, extends range
note: Extends range from 20 to 50 km. Wrong spacing causes new problems. Crosstalk increases.

name: Spark transmitter
note: Spark gap must erode uniformly; motor-driven rotation prevents pitting. Emission is damped wave.

name: Coherer detector
note: A tube of glass filled with iron filings between two metal plugs. When RF current (from a radio signal) passes through, the filings cohere (stick together), dropping resistance from 1 megohm to 1000 ohms. A relay responds to this current change, signalling the received dot or dash. After each signal, a tapper mechanically shakes the tube to decohere the filings. Unreliable and slow (tapping delay), but it was the only radio detector before solid-state rectifiers.

name: Crystal detector
note: Cat's whisker point must be pressed precisely. Temperamental but much more reliable than coherer.

name: Tuned LC circuit
kb: Inductor and capacitor in series or parallel; resonance at specific frequency
note: Resonance sharpest with low resistance; high Q demands low loss. Variable capacitor tunes band.

name: Continuous wave transmitter
note: CW is narrower bandwidth than spark. Regenerative circuits required. Frequency drift is problem.

name: Triode oscillator
note: A triode with feedback can generate any frequency from audio (10 Hz) to microwave (1000 MHz), tuned by the LC circuit. The oscillation amplitude is limited by the triode's power supply and efficiency. Used in radio transmitters, local oscillators for superheterodyne receivers, and audio oscillators for music synthesis. The triode is THE electronic oscillator until solid-state transistors arrive.
_internal: [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1e3 added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: vacuum tube oscillator needs high vacuum for electron operation]

name: Amplitude modulation
note: A microphone signal (audio, 0-10 kHz) is added to the RF oscillator output, varying its amplitude. The modulated wave is transmitted; a receiver detects the envelope (the modulation) using a rectifier, recovering audio. The trick: a 1 MHz carrier modulated with 1 kHz audio produces sidebands at 999 kHz and 1001 kHz. Radio stations are spaced 10 kHz apart (AM broadcast). The bandwidth is about 2x the audio frequency. Simple and robust.

name: Superheterodyne receiver
note: Instead of amplifying the RF signal directly (hard at high frequencies), a mixer combines the received signal with a local oscillator, producing a difference frequency (intermediate frequency, typically 455 kHz or 10.7 MHz). Tuning changes only the local oscillator; the intermediate frequency is fixed and easy to amplify. This is the most important radio innovation after AM: it made high-gain, selective receivers practical. Nearly all radio since 1920 is superheterodyne.

name: Frequency modulation
note: Audio signal varies the frequency of the RF carrier instead of the amplitude. A 100 MHz carrier modulated with 1 kHz audio swings ±75 kHz. FM is immune to amplitude noise (static, ignition noise), so reception is much quieter. Bandwidth is about 10x wider than AM (200 kHz for 15 kHz audio), requiring wider channel spacing. Requires sophisticated receivers (discriminators, limiters). Adopted late (1940s in consumer radio) due to infrastructure cost, but ultimately superior.

name: Dipole antenna
note: Radiation resistance low; matching essential. Overhead antenna key; ground connection less important.

name: Radio direction finding
note: Null sharper than maximum; bearing error a few degrees. Two RDFs triangulate position.

name: Radar
kb: Pulse transmitter and receiver with CRT display, shows range and bearing to reflective objects
note: Pulse timing must be precise. CRT displays return. Critical for aircraft detection. Extremely difficult.

name: Cathode ray tube
note: An evacuated glass tube with a heated cathode that emits electrons, accelerated by 10,000 V towards a phosphor-coated anode. The electron beam is steered by magnetic coils (X and Y deflection). Where the beam hits the screen, the phosphor glows. Varying the beam current modulates the brightness. This is the display technology that made electronic television possible. The key: the beam is fast (MHz), allowing full-screen raster scanning at video rate.
_internal: [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1e3 added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: evacuated tube for electron beam display requires high vacuum]

name: Television by mechanical scanning
note: Disc must rotate precisely; flicker is problem at low frame rates. Extremely dim picture.

name: Iconoscope camera tube
note: Mosaic target must have fine structure. Capacitive coupling to each cell critical.

name: Video scanning standard
note: Frame rate matched to power line frequency. Sync timing allows receiver lock. Adoption slow.

name: Facsimile transmission
note: Sender and receiver synchronisation must be perfect. Scanning speed trades resolution for time.

name: Punched card
note: Card format is 80 columns, 12 rows; de facto standard. Holes read by mechanical sensing.

name: Jacquard card chain
note: Card-driven loom reduces pattern complexity. Thousands of cards weave complex fabrics. Precursor to computing.

name: Hollerith tabulator
note: Uses reading brushes that sense hole positions. Census processing time falls from years to weeks.

name: Card sorter
note: Solenoid plunger must be fast and strong. Cards must not jam. Sorting seconds per card.

name: Keypunch machine
note: Card held precisely during punch. Operator verifies key before strike. Jams common.

name: Adding machine
note: Carry mechanism critical; each decade must propagate carry. Addition only, not multiplication.

name: Comptometer
note: Instead of a crank (one operation per second), the Comptometer (1887 onward) uses keys (one per digit). Pressing a key lever multiple times increments that digit, accumulating the sum. Touch typists could use Comptometers almost as fast as they thought of numbers. Faster than Arithmometer. The innovation is that the operator interface is ergonomic and intuitive (press 5 five times to add 5), not just mechanical optimization.

name: Cash register
note: Mechanical register prevents underring. Solenoid locks drawer. Counter records every transaction.

name: Slide rule
note: Two wooden rules with logarithmic scales, aligned by hand and compared visually. To multiply 5*7, you find 5 on one scale and 7 on the other, align them, and read 35 off the fixed scale. Uses the log identity: log(a*b)=log(a)+log(b). Accuracy is 3 digits, good enough for engineering work. Ubiquitous by 1900, slide rules were the dominant calculation tool until electronic calculators (1970s). Simple, cheap, and fast enough for design iteration.

name: Index card and filing system
note: 3 by 5 inch card is standard. Filing order discipline essential. Improvement over bound ledgers.

name: Dewey decimal classification
note: System is hierarchical; all zeros are philosophy. Allows insertion without renumbering.
